reference.title: Musée entomologique illustré: Les insectes, Orthoptères plate I

doc: *Gryllus campestris*, dorsal — the field cricket, male.
The archive's first Orthoptera, and the first plate whose order had to be
added to `PLATE_ORDERS` and `REQUIRED_PARTS`. Traced from the Orthoptères
plate of the *Musée entomologique illustré* (1878), where the cricket is
named in the margin and shares the sheet with a mole cricket, two earwigs
and a cockroach. `references/gryllus-campestris.jpg` is the plate.
## The reference is not a dorsal figure, and that had to be worked round
This is the only reference in the folder that is a *habitat scene* rather
than a specimen figure: the animals are drawn among bindweed and grass, lit,
and posed. The cricket is seen from above and a little behind — close to
dorsal, and not square to it.
So what came off the plate is the arrangement: where the pronotum ends and
the tegmina begin, how far the hind femur reaches, how the antennae sweep
back, that the tegminal venation is coarse enough to count. The
*proportions* were then taken from the published measurements — 19 to 27 mm
long, about a third as wide as long — because a foreshortened figure cannot
give them and guessing from one would have made the animal too short. That
is a weaker provenance than the other fifteen plates have and it is recorded
here rather than left for somebody to notice.
## What the drawing has to get right
The **tegmina**: leathery forewings lying flat over the abdomen, one
overlapping the other, with venation coarse enough to draw. They are the
reason `WING_COVERS` gained a `tegmina` state — a cricket's forewings are
not the hard cases of a beetle and not the clear membrane of a wasp, and
making the record answer either would have been making it lie.
The **stridulatory field** on the tegmen — the harp and the oval mirror a
male rubs to sing — is drawn as one cell, because it is the reason this
plate commits to a sex and because a field cricket is far more often heard
than seen.
Then the **hind femur**, which is a third of the animal and three times the
depth of any other limb here. Drawn at the ground beetle's proportions a
cricket cannot jump, and a saltatorial leg is the character that puts it in
this order at a glance.
Then the **cerci**: the two long tails at the tip of the abdomen. They are
the part `REQUIRED_PARTS.orthoptera` asks for that no other order does, and
`cercus` had been sitting in `PLATE_PART_IDS` unused since the schema was
written, with a comment saying it was for a cricket's tails.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front of the head, y = 1000 at the tip of the abdomen. Pronotum
210 to 420, tegmina 410 to 900. The cerci reach y = 1210 and the antennae
out to x = 520 and above y = -360.

note: The legs first, so they pass under the body.
The hind femur is the whole point of the order: 130 units deep against 44
for the fore femur, which is the ratio the measurements give and roughly
what the reference shows. Everything a cricket does that a beetle cannot
is in that shape.
The abdomen, drawn before the tegmina so they lie over it. Only its last
two segments and the cerci show on the finished plate, which is what a
cricket at rest looks like from above.
A cercus, in two joints. The pair of them is what `REQUIRED_PARTS` asks
this order for and no other, and they are longer than they look — nearly
a quarter of the animal past the tip of the abdomen.
One tegmen: a leathery forewing lying flat over the abdomen. Authored
from the midline out, so the renderer's reflection supplies the other —
which is a small lie, because on the animal one tegmen overlaps the other
and they are not symmetric. A plate that drew the overlap would have to
choose a side, and the character a reader is being shown is that the
covers are leathery and flat rather than which of them is on top.
The venation, which on a tegmen is coarse enough to draw stroke for
stroke rather than suggested — five lengthwise, four across.
The pale patch at the base of the tegmen — yellow on the animal, and the
one bright mark on a cricket that is otherwise glossy black.
The mirror: the oval cell in the stridulatory field that a male rubs to
sing, and the reason this plate commits to a sex. A field cricket is
heard far more often than it is seen, and this is the organ that does it.
The pronotum: a transverse saddle with almost straight sides, and shorter
than it is wide. A cricket has no scutellum, which is why
`REQUIRED_PARTS.orthoptera` does not ask for one.
The head: large, rounded and as wide as the pronotum, which is a cricket
and not a grasshopper — a grasshopper's head is drawn out and slanted.
The three ocelli, in a line across the face between the compound eyes:
one on the midline, drawn once, and a pair either side of it.
The antenna. Filiform and very long — as long as the body on the animal,
and about three quarters of it here, because the frame is measured from
the drawing and a full-length pair would leave the cricket small in the
middle of a mostly empty box.
Three open strokes rather than a chain of joints: the segments are far too
fine to draw, and what has to read is the sweep.
